chapter: New York, Henderson and Charlie Johnson
title: Why Charlie Johnson stayed obscure: Small's, no radio, dying at the Lafayette
summary: Johnson stayed at Small's for years with no broadcasts, wrote hokum like 'Fat and Greasy' to get heard, and the band died at the Lafayette Theater despite its quality.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Well tell me a little bit about Charlie
Johnson, Herman. He's a guy who really never has gotten as much publicity as he deserved.

He -- right. Right, right, because he wrote a lot of tunes before I met him. I heard him talking about them. 'Fat and Greasy is one thing he did. Naturally that was for the -- you know, the gutter, for these -- but he did a lot of nice things, did, and I never heard about -- he didn't hear about either, because I don't know, at that time -- hm, let's face it, a colored guy couldn't get out. And you had to right some hokum, some junk, something like 'Fat and Greasy' before they considered it, maybe, and it stinks, and I mean -- 'Fat and Greasy'. Who wants it? Who needs it? You know.
And he was a good musician, good piano player, and I'm trying to think of --

For example, Herman, we take three guys who are contemporary then. Let's take Fletcher Henderson, Duke Ellington, and Charlie Johnson, all of whom had good bands, and yet Charlie Johnson is the least known of the three.
Yes.
What -- why would that be?
Well, I would think that Charlie stayed in Small's so many years, because he's -- he -- I don't know how they met, when, but Charlie stayed there so many years.

I mean it's one of those things. Stay here, this is home. (unintelligible). You don't have to worry, have to run out on the road like those other guys, out, not [ ], not going to pay you, you don't say that. I ain't going to pay you nothing, but stay here, you know what I mean, you know. Forty years and you'll always have a job, and I'll be a millionaire, you know. Because you know, just like down some places, still going downtown, 54th Street, Ryan's, you know.
You stay here and work, and you can go out and work when you get ready, but come on back and we'll be here, and I hope you can make it back, you know?
But still, Charlie had a hell of a band.
Well he did have a hell of a band. Red Allen, Louie Armstrong, he's had some of the best people you can name, at one time.
Was Louie with him?
Oh sure. Louie worked in there --
How about that.
Heck yeah.
Well, was there a -- did you -- was there a wire, radio wire in Smalls?
Well, a couple or few small times there they had this connection with the radio station, where --
But not --
-- they would broadcast, but it wasn't --
Well it wasn't like the Cotton Club, or Duke was on the air every night, or something like that.
No, no, no. No, no.
Or Fletcher with Roseland Ballroom.
No, no. No.
Well was this what made the difference, do you think, the difference in --

No, well that -- and the money, the it might have an interest. There wasn't nobody gived a damn. Let's face it, you know. The more you're in front of the public, naturally the more the public hears you. But nobody gave a damn, and they spend their money, and that was it.
Even though it was a hell of a band.
Oh, yes, sure, hell of a band. And he came out, and went in the Apollo Theater, and died like a dog. I was with him.
Really? He did?
Oh sure. I was in the band. We went -- not the Apollo, Lafayette. That's before the Apollo. I was in the band. And --
But even within the community of Harlem he wasn't that well known.
Well it wasn't that he wasn't well-known, maybe, it's what's happening. I mean if you can't get
